newsitem.title: MEXICO: Pension delay seen helping gov't 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Pension delay seen helping gov't 1997 budget.

text.p: Mexico hopes a delay to its new privatized pension fund system will help its 1997 budget with the continued flow of funds into government coffers, analysts and legislators said Tuesday.

President Ernesto Zedillo sent a bill to Congress this week that would delay for six months the entry of funds into newly-formed private pension companies, a move that will replace the country's virtually bankrupt pay-as-you-go state system.
The bill was part of the new pact between government, business and labor that outlines economic policy for 1997.

"A delay in the application of the new Social Security law could represent a savings of 50 percent in the outlay (for 1997) of what it will cost the government to restructure the pension system," said Miguel Angel Saenz, a legislator on the Social Security Commission in the Chamber of Deputies.

He said the Mexican government would need to spend about 1.5 percent of 1997 gross national product to continue paying pensions to 1.5 million retirees in the social security system without new funding from current workers.
Waiting six months will save the government 7.5 billion pesos from next year's budget, he said.
But the political cost of such a delay could weigh more heavily on the nation, as foreigners eyeing the market see the move as yet another obstacle in a series of delayed and revised privatizations.
Mexico recently backtracked on selling off its petrochemicals industry and has also been badly delayed in selling its railroads.
Marcos Chavez, an economist at the Colegio de Mexico, said the delay reflects the government's worries about the cost of getting the new system underway.
"The government has a deficit problem next year due to the increase in public debt payments, a problem exacerbated by the pension fund costs. The government is clearly searching for time," he said.

Although the National Savings Commission (Consar) said the privatization of the nation's retirement funds is on track, officials acknowledged the schedule change will force adjustments for companies planning to operate local retirement funds, known as Afores.
"Instead of receiving the money on a certain date they will receive it in another and this will simply have to be adjusted," said Juan Manuel Carreras, technical secretary of the Consar.
Emerging fund managers, generally unions of Mexican, United States and Chilean firms, would begin hiring and advertising for the pension fund companies as scheduled.
Carreras said the delay aims to solve technical problems in the codes retirees use to access their accounts, such as eliminating duplicate access codes.

"The first entry of revenue corresponding to the new pension fund system will be be passed to the second semester, for reasons fundamentally to refine collection systems," he added. The Consar estimates 30 billion pesos will enter the new pension fund system.
